quietus.title: King Ayisoba – Pure Confusion
quietus.description: King Ayisoba Pure Confusion King Ayisoba's seventh album was cut live in a single sitting. Everything else was built around it afterwards Pure Confusion by King Ayisoba The most useful thing to know about Pure Confusion is how it was made. King Ayisoba flew to England in November 2024, sat down in Adrian Sherwood’s studio in Ramsgate, and played the whole record in one afternoon. He says the songs were already finished in his head. Nothing about his performance was altered after the fact. The bass, the cello, the saxophone, the harmonica, the dub processing on the desk: all of it was added later, to a recording of a man who was alone in a room with a two-string lute made from a calabash...

quietus.title: High on Dynamite: the rapid rise & fall of The White Panthers (UK)
quietus.description: In an extract from the new book International Freak, author M. Syd Rosen describes a doomed attempt in 1970 to ignite a revolution with rock & roll White Panthers EP by Robin Farquharson & The White Panthers Born in 1930 into a privileged South African family, Robin Farquharson was part of a new wave of intellectuals who tasked themselves with reimagining society in the wake of World War II until everything fell apart. Watched by the secret police and hampered by mounting paranoia, Farquharson fled to 1960s London and tried to reinvent himself as a countercultural guru. In 1970 the writer and would-be revolutionary recorded a single dedicated to the Palestinian hijacker Leila Khaled, then…

quietus.title: Adapt or Don’t: Marc Almond Interviewed
quietus.description: Marc Almond meets Patrick Clarke in Soho to discuss the death of Dave Ball, the final Soft Cell album Danceteria and his career as a shapeshifter Photo by Mike Owen I meet Marc Almond a few minutes’ walk from the Brewer Street flat in which he lived in the early 1980s. There is a longstanding urban myth that a pet boa constrictor once escaped from it and into the Soho sewers where it slithers to this day, although Almond clarifies that it only got as far as terrorising the neighbours. “I think it got out through the piping and came out through their toilet. I got a warning from the police saying, ‘Please look after your boa constrictor!’” The point stands, however, that...

quietus.title: Carmen Villain – Memoria
quietus.description: Carmen Villain Memoria New Carmen Villain shares its slow-burning intensity with the Apichatpong Weerasethakul film it shares a title with Memoria by Carmen Villain Carmen Villain’s fifth album, Memoria begins in familiar territory: flute tones stretch out across an enormous, reverberant field, the same patient sound that defined her last record. It doesn't stay there long. Within a couple of minutes the ground shifts, and the record makes its real statement: this is not music built for casual listening. Sharing its title with Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s languorous 2021 film, this is a record made for the kind of slow, attentive surrender that lets its details bloom. Where 2022’s Only Love…

quietus.title: Dressed in a Leotard: How Suede Wrote – and Abandoned – a Ballet
quietus.description: An extract from Rodge Glass' new biography of the second half of Suede's existence reveals how the band recently wrote a score and songs for a ballet, in part inspired by The Fall's work with Michael Clark Band reformations frequently offer thin creative gruel. Even if new material is made, it’s often scattered apologetically at the start of gigs before the price-gouged audience get a dose of nostalgia, a shot in the arm to take them fleetingly back to the heady hormonal years of teenagerhood. Suede were at such a low ebb when they split in 2003 that their return had to be done differently, and done right – avoiding what Brett Anderson describes as “the living death of playing exclusively…

quietus.title: This Must Be The Place: Do We Have A Right To Housing?
quietus.description: In an exclusive extract from his new book, A Right to Housing, Samuel Stein argues that the struggle for affordable housing is an inseparable element of the class struggle Photo by Jonathan Billinger. Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0. When most people think of a right to housing, they are conceiving of a right to a home – a city, nation, or world where no one is pushed into homelessness, and where no one is evicted because of tenant poverty or landlord avarice. A right to a home means ensuring there is always enough housing for everyone, regardless of market conditions. It is not a right to real estate, or an entitlement to for-profit homeownership – a recipe for the kind of…

quietus.title: Music With You: 12 Kylie Deep Cuts
quietus.description: To celebrate the imminent publication of his new book Can’t Get You Out Of My Head: In Search of Kylie, Michael Cragg treats us to a rundown of a dozen of the Queen of Pop's lesser-known bops Having spent the last two years thinking non-stop about Kylie Ann Minogue, I feel like I know her discography pretty well. I’m also aware that for some a ‘Kylie deep cut’ is probably a song like 2004’s ‘Chocolate’, which actually reached the top 10, while for the many true obsessives we’re talking ‘Sometime Samurai’, Kylie’s other super odd collaboration with Japanese artist Towa Tei. Basically what I’m saying is you can’t please everyone, so across this list of 12 Kylie deep cuts I’ve focused...

quietus.title: Semibreve Finalises Lineup with Films, Talks, Installations and More
quietus.description: The opening night will also feature a mystery gig from an as-yet unannounced performer Matthew Biederman, the winner of the Edigma Semibreve Award 2026 Braga's Semibreve festival has completed the lineup for this year's event with the addition of a host of installations, films, talks and masterclasses. The festival has also announced that its opening night will feature a special performance from a yet-to-be-announced artist, whose identity will be concealed until they take to the stage at the Basílica Dos Congregados. Running from 22 to 25 October, a music line-up that includes a rare set from composer Nuno Canavarro, Flora Yin-Wong, Fennesz, Marta Salogni and more, was finalised earlier…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Bonnie ‘Prince’ Billy :: Ghosts of American Psychonauts
aquariumdrunkard.description: Bonnie ‘Prince’ Billy’s live show can be any number of things—a solo acoustic ramble through covers and oddities and absurd stories, an electrified duo with Superwolves’ Matt Sweeney, or, occasionally, and if you’re lucky, a full-band interpretation of old and new songs that makes you think of them in new contexts. Ghosts of American Psychonauts is very much the latter, eight songs recorded at the Pico Union Project in Los Angeles in February 2025...

aquariumdrunkard.title: Nick Jonah Davis :: Rose Delta Rising
aquariumdrunkard.description: You might find yourself succumbing to shorthand hyperbole when trying to describe Rose Delta Rising , Nick Jonah Davis’ remarkable new album. Ry Cooder joining Pentangle? Peter Green playing on Bryter Layter? Sonic Youth covering Avocet? Rose Delta Rising can stand up to any such fanciful daydreams, but it adds up to much more than just music nerd wish fulfillment, delivering a highly personalized and singular listening experience.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Well Travelled :: Talk Talk’s Final Live Performances 40 Years On
aquariumdrunkard.description: With In Another World: The Four Seasons of Talk Talk , music writer Graeme Thomson charts one of the most mystical trajectories ever undertaken by a one-time pop band. Today marks the 40th anniversary of the band's final live performance in Spain. To commemorate, we're pleased to share an edited extract from In Another World.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Crying Laughing :: Talking
aquariumdrunkard.description: Strange and turbulent times call for insistent new theme songs and rallying cries. On Talking , Baltimore’s Crying Laughing answer the call with necessary and emphatic instrumental anthems, driven by a twin alto sax attack and percussion that channels the snap and bounce of New Orleans rhythms. The result feels tightly interlocked, yet constantly in motion.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Mike D :: Thank You
aquariumdrunkard.description: Thank You , the first solo work from Mike D, ascribed to the appellation Mike D 5D. Though he hasn’t been too far from music, producing records for Portugal. The Man and Soft Play, the album follows a long period of creative grief. But the work of his sons Davis and Skyler Diamond and their circle of friends have drawn the wildest Beastie back to writing and performing once again.

aquariumdrunkard.title: The Lagniappe Sessions :: Maisy Owen
aquariumdrunkard.description: For her debut Lagniappe Session, Maisy Owen turns to four songwriters who share her gift for making difficult things sound beautiful. From Rosa Lee Carson’s devastating “The Drinker’s Child,” written when Carson was just fourteen, to Townes Van Zandt’s “Snowin’ on Raton,” David Olney’s “Deeper Well,” and Amy Winehouse’s “What Is It About Men,” Owen follows a thread through country, folk and soul-pop songwriting, finding a sweetness in songs that are anything but sweet.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Secular Music Group :: Volume 3
aquariumdrunkard.description: Since emerging out of the wilds of Connecticut a few years back, SMG have released three LPs worth of rapturous sounds, each moment filled with pure melody, meditative rhythm and immersive textures, all captured wondrously on vintage 4-track ¼” tape. It’s like Gil Evans arranging an album by Natural Information Society, finding a perfect blend of gorgeously pastel hues and minimalist restraint.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Diles Que No Me Maten :: Escrito en Agua
aquariumdrunkard.description: The Mexico City based five-piece Diles Que No Me Maten conjure a languid and mournful psychedelia on their fourth album, Escrito en Agua , infusing krautrock and slowcore elements into a patiently unfolding album that sears with intensity.

mubi.title: Defending the Elusive
mubi.description: Last Year in Marienbad (Alain Resnais, 1961). 1 Although it’s seldom acknowledged, one of the supreme pleasures of movies is the confusion and uncertainty often prompted by the beginning of a story, when we’re not yet fully tuned in to what’s going on. As in our sleeping dreams, a sense of infinite possibility stretches before us. That seemingly limitless vista soon disappoints once it is foreshortened into something real and recognizable, such as a place, an environment, a mood, a character, a theme, a genre, or a plot. Yet without these comfortable anchors, something that resembles prenatal bliss envelops our ignorance, and the fact that we can imagine almost anything makes the start of…

mubi.title: Venice Dispatch: The Garden of Forking Paths
mubi.description: NAZA (Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, 2026). To watch my first film at the 83rd Venice Film Festival, I wore a VR headset. I say “watch” when the more accurate verb would be “experience,” at least going by the fest’s preferred vocabulary for what goes down on Lazzaretto Vecchio, an island a stone’s throw away from the Lido. Once used as a checkpoint for Holy Land pilgrims, and then—after the plague reached the lagoon in 1423—a leper colony, it is, in 2026 AD, now home to the virtual reality sidebar. The architecture has barely changed through the centuries. Dotting the high-ceilinged corridors that used to house the city’s moribund, festival guests can find various booths, each promising…

mubi.title: Survival Tactics: A Locarno Critics Academy Correspondence
mubi.description: Notebook, in partnership with the Locarno Critics Academy, presents a series of critical correspondences in which this year’s participants look back at the Swiss film festival. In this final installment, three critics explore how “tendenko,” a Japanese term that implies isolating to survive a tsunami, resonated across the program. “We live in a state of apocalyptic fetishism,” a radio announcer proclaims in Ann Oren’s Objet A (2026), and the slate of films at Locarno this August did little to dissuade its spectators of this assessment. As has been everywhere observed in recent years, the constant sounding of the alarm has become the 21st century’s room tone, and film festivals are not…

mubi.title: Cut and Spliced: A Locarno Critics Academy Correspondence
mubi.description: Notebook, in partnership with the Locarno Critics Academy, presents a series of critical correspondences in which this year’s participants look back at the Swiss film festival. In this second installment, four critics muse on cinema’s ability to splice disparate fragments together. They touch on ecstatic New York sirens, self-preservation in Iran and Palestine, performances that bear the weight of passing time, and an actress’s descent into two-faced delirium in Rome. We hear in Sans soleil (1983) that “Nothing sorts out memories from ordinary moments. It is only later that they claim remembrance, when they show their scars.” This is how I feel about memories all the time. What lingers in…

mubi.title: Rushes | Remembering Dolly Parton, A24 Teases Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes Doc, the 100 Most-Screened Films in NYC
mubi.description: Get in touch to send in cinephile news and discoveries. To keep up with our latest features, sign up for the Weekly Edit newsletter and follow us @mubinotebook on X and Instagram . NEWS Primtime (Lance Oppenheim, 2026). Meryl Streep and Laura Poitras have come aboard as executive producers on Julia Loktev’s upcoming documentary My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile (2026) , the second part of Loktev’s profile of independent Russian journalists operating in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine, which recently had its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival. In a statement, Streep describes Loktev as “the Samuel Pepys of Putin’s Russia” and describes her films as a “blazing achievement.”…

mubi.title: It Was Once Fire: A Locarno Critics Academy Correspondence
mubi.description: Notebook, in partnership with the Locarno Critics Academy, presents a series of critical correspondences in which this year's participants look back at the Swiss film festival. In this first installment, letters exchanged between three critics contour what was on screen—broken relations, recalcitrant presences—with their experiences of Locarno beyond the frame. Photo by Alyssandra Maxine. Dear Vedant and Max, I’m writing you from the real world, which is to say, from my desk in my apartment in Brooklyn. The first few days of the festival seem very far away now, as they did even when I last saw you only five days ago. During a festival, time tends to go by like that: very quickly and also…

mubi.title: The Final Temenos
mubi.description: Photo by Emma Fuchs. At sunset we move like a herd. Arms laden with blankets, we snake down the gravel path, as signs in blue spray paint warn “ΠΡΟΣΟΧΗ! Use Caution!” Halfway there, the trees that bracket us part like curtains. Below, stark against the green-gold valley, we can make out a small white square—the projection screen. At a fork in the path, there is a small sign with a blue arrow on it, and the word “Temenos.” From here, the path narrows until suddenly it opens onto a clearing. In a small field, like a basin, rows of red beanbag chairs dot the ground in front of the screen, and behind them, a crescent of pink cushioned benches and a projector wait. The restoration of Eniaios…

mubi.title: The Armchair Answer to the Troubles
mubi.description: Illustration by Danny Ische. The 1970s was a difficult decade for cinemas across Britain and Ireland as attendances continued their long postwar decline. Most of the glamorous art deco picture palaces built during the 1930s had either closed or fallen into disrepair and comparatively few new cinemas were opened after World War II until the arrival of the multiplexes in the 1980s. While these challenges were facing exhibitors in many other countries around the world, Northern Ireland’s experience of the downturn was unique. The outbreak of violent sectarian conflict in the late 1960s, euphemistically known as the Troubles, created an environment that actively discouraged cinema attendance.…

Inspector Ginko (Michel Piccoli) has orchestrated a spectacular motorcade to transport a large sum of banknotes; only, this motorcade is not carrying any actual banknotes at all; they are merely the diversion that Ginko has […]

Films had always been made in New Zealand, but they were largely foreign productions, with a cast and crew of professionals brought into the country. At […]

Bulbs were being sold for more than most farmers’ houses, as fortunes were won, lost, and gambled anew. […]

publicdomainreview.title: “Worthless Idiot, Donkey Head”: Parodies of Pedantry on the Renaissance Stage
publicdomainreview.description: Pompous know-it-alls were once a mainstay of mockery on the Italian stage. Arnoud Visser investigates this stock character of the pedant and his association with individual superiority, social distinction, and sexual transgression, finding a form of satire that took aim at the Renaissance humanist’s erudition and lofty ideals.
